name: Testing a Tutor Before Students Use It
title: Testing a Tutor Before Students Use It
answer: Every tutor a school sets up should be tested before any student uses it, with a teacher acting as a struggling student who asks for answers, makes common mistakes, and tries to get the tool to do the work. The test takes about half an hour and catches problems that could otherwise affect a whole class. Testing also checks the tutor's own explanations for accuracy, and the results should be written down so other teachers and the district can reuse what was learned.

sections.body: This idea is a pre flight check for a configured tutor, done by a teacher before students ever log in. The teacher deliberately plays the part of a struggling student, requesting answers outright, making typical errors, and pushing the tool to complete the work for them. If the tutor gives in to any of this, the setup is not ready and needs more work. The problem it solves is that a flawed setup, left untested, can shape how an entire class learns and can be hard to undo once students have used it. A short test up front prevents that damage at very little cost in time.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In any grade band, the teacher who will run the tutor spends roughly half an hour in the student role before the class uses it. They ask for answers directly, make the mistakes students commonly make, and try to get the tool to do the work, then note where it gives in. They also ask the tutor to explain the lesson's key ideas and check those explanations for accuracy. After this, a short trial with a few students before full use can surface problems that the teacher's own testing missed. The written results, covering what was tested, what went wrong, and what changed, are passed on so the next teacher setting up a similar tool does not start from scratch.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea as practice supported by research. It cites research on a carefully designed math tutor which found that real classroom use revealed problems that computer simulations had missed (Looi et al., 2026). The text does not report a size, a score, or any other figure from that work. The claim drawn from it is modest: a short trial with a few students before full use can catch the same kind of problems that simulations overlook. The half hour teacher test is presented as practical guidance rather than as a measured finding.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are set by the text itself. Testing is not a guarantee, and the book treats it as a way to reduce risk rather than remove it, which is why a short trial with a few students is still recommended before full use. The teacher keeps the judgment about whether the setup is ready, since only a person can decide that the tool has given in or that an explanation is wrong. The written note is a record for colleagues, not a formal approval, and the district's shared set of tested setups is described as saving time and raising quality, not as a substitute for each teacher's own check. Nothing in the text addresses privacy, consent, or legal duties, so those decisions remain with the school and are outside what this idea covers.
